anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks and block or deadlock each other, stalling progress at the lock-manager layer. 
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions compete for hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, forcing serialization below the lock layer. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process exhausts kernel-enforced limits such as file handles, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or thread quotas, preventing new allocations.

When all three root causes arise together, the system exhibits compound symptoms: long lock-wait chains mixed with high buffer-busy/latch wait events, CPU spin with no throughput gain, spikes of deadlock victim rollbacks, and surging connection-pool backlogs. Simultaneously, the engine begins to log failures to create threads, allocate shared memory, or open files; new sessions, background workers, or parallel tasks are intermittently rejected even as existing ones hang on locks or latches. Latency becomes unpredictable, throughput collapses, and monitoring views show ballooning lock queues, latch waits, and kernel-level allocation errors, making it difficult to isolate any single bottleneck.

Causal chain: intense lock contention leaves transactions open longer, multiplying the number of concurrent sessions and pinned buffer pages. The enlarged session count and page churn amplify hot-page and latch competition inside the buffer manager. As workers spin or wait, they consume additional kernel objects—threads, file descriptors, async-I/O contexts—which pushes the process toward or beyond operating-system limits. Once limits are hit, the engine fails to spawn the very background tasks (e.g., deadlock detectors, checkpointers, flushers) needed to relieve lock and buffer pressure, further prolonging locks and latches and causing positive feedback that rapidly degrades the entire workload.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
